title: Is there a scientific formula for funny?
summary: A live-audience episode asking whether there is a scientific formula for humor. Josh and Chuck open with the Richard Wiseman LaughLab "world's funniest joke" project, then survey how philosophers (Aristotle, Plato, Schopenhauer, Kant) and Freud explained laughter. They cover the superiority, inferiority, relief, and incongruity theories, the benign violation idea, and "parapraxis"-style twist jokes. They discuss the too-soon line in comedy (Gilbert Godfrey, Portlandia, Timothy Hutton's Groupon ad), brain research on joke detection and appreciation using fMRI, the dopamine reward system, and frontal-lobe damage affecting joke comprehension. They also cover Christopher Hitchens' claim about women and humor, gender and national humor differences, the brown-nose effect, and Robert Provine's research on everyday laughter. A tongue-in-cheek "formula" is mentioned, and the episode is closed with a plug for a HowStuffWorks article. Includes a Toyota Corolla sponsor read at the start and a mid-episode break.

segments.title: Opening banter and sponsor read
segments.summary: Toyota Corolla sponsor read, then the hosts introduce the question of whether a scientific formula for funny exists and recount Richard Wiseman's LaughLab world's funniest joke project.

segments.title: Animal laughter and the social nature of laughing
segments.summary: Aristotle thought only humans laugh, but chimpanzees, apes, and rats laugh when tickled. Laughter is a basic vocal pattern shared across cultures, involves facial muscles, and people laugh far more in groups than alone. Humor itself varies by culture, place, and time.

segments.title: Short jokes, Kardashian philosophy parody, and Jack Handy
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Schopenhauer's dark humor, a parody Twitter feed mixing Schopenhauer with Kim Kardashian's tweets, and Jack Handy's short jokes, including the 'I came here in peace' line. They mention a joke formula found online that doesn't settle the question.

segments.title: Chris Rock on what is funny and the field of humor studies
segments.summary: Chris Rock's quip that thinking about what is funny ruins it is mentioned. The hosts note humor studies is not taken seriously by many psychologists but has a scientific community, the International Society for Humor Studies, and brain imaging has added evidence.

segments.title: Superiority, inferiority, and relief theories of humor
segments.summary: The hosts review the main philosophical theories: superiority (Plato, Aristotle, Hobbes), inferiority (laughing at a fall and seeing yourself in it), and Freud's relief theory of released pent-up energy, with self-deprecation given as an example.

segments.title: Incongruity theory, parapraxdokian, and the Aristocrats
segments.summary: Kant's incongruity idea is explained, with The Aristocrats joke as an example. Figures of speech such as Groucho Marx, Homer Simpson, and Mitch Hedberg jokes are used to show expectation-breaking humor. The hosts coin 'parapraxdokian' for a twist that makes the audience rethink the setup.

segments.title: Benign violation theory and too-soon jokes
segments.summary: The benign violation theory combines the main theories. The hosts discuss the line between funny and offensive, too-soon jokes, Gilbert Godfrey's tweet, a Portlandia 9/11 sketch, and Timothy Hutton's Groupon ad.

segments.title: Brain science: joke detection, dopamine, and frontal lobe damage
segments.summary: fMRI studies show joke detection occurs in the left hemisphere, with different regions for puns (language areas), setup-punchline jokes (frontal lobe), and reward via the amygdala and dopamine. Frontal lobe damage can impair joke understanding. Low mood can block laughter, and laughing fits involve spindle cells.

segments.title: Gender differences, national humor, brown-nosing, and everyday laughter
segments.summary: Christopher Hitchens' Vanity Fair argument that women are not as funny is discussed, along with Washington University research on sex differences in reward response. The hosts cover British versus American humor, the brown-nose effect where subordinates laugh more at bosses, and Robert Provine's finding that most daily laughter is not at jokes.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts plug the HowStuffWorks article on the topic, note there is no listener mail, and sign off with a Toyota Corolla sponsor line.
